latin.189:
§. VI.
Dissensus ad Fastigium pervenit quando, paulò post Formulam Concordiae in lucem publicam editam, cujus Historia satis superque nota, Sententiam de Praedestinatione inde ab Augustini temporibus Occidentali Ecclesiae tantùm non Universa, etiam Reformatoribus ejus primis utriusque Protestantium partis, Luthero Zwinglio, utpote Augustini & Thomae Aquinatis Discipulis, receptam, Ægidius Hunnius oppugnavit,
latin.190: & Patrum Augustino antiquiorum opinionem amplectendam suasit.
latin.191: Enimverò ab hoc tempore, Hunnium plerique Lutheranorum sequuti sunt, Reformatis utplurimùm Augustinianae Doctrinae constanter insistentibus.
latin.192: Nostri (inquit saepius laudatus Calixtus) è quibus olim multi itidem Absolutum Decretum approbarunt, paulatim ad Sententiam primorum Quatuor Seculorum (nempe Decretum juxta praescientiam factum) sese receperunt, qua in re multùm & egregiè laboravit Ægidius Hunnius:
latin.193: Difficile autem est, Sententiam hanc ita proponere, ne quid Pelagianismo affine habere videatur, quemadmodum sanè Pelagianismi Hunnium accusant, tum Daniel Tossanus Calvinista, tùm Adamus Tannerus Jesuita. cit. loc, num. 22. Confer ejusdem Calixti Considerat. Doct. Reform, juxta Confess. Thoruniens. de Gratia p. 62.
latin.194: interim nec hunc, nec antecedentium Dissensuum quemquam, Fundamentalem arbitrati, Tractatuló priori à num. 23. ad 35. num. 45. & à num. 76. ad 82, inclusivè.

pass_a.189: §. VI. The Dissensus arrived at its Peak when, a little after the Formula of Concord had been brought into public light — whose History is known more than enough — Aegidius Hunnius attacked the Sentence concerning Predestination which, from the times of Augustine onward, had been received by the Western Church as all but Universal, and also by its first Reformers of either party of the Protestants, Luther and Zwingli, as being disciples of Augustine and of Thomas Aquinas,
pass_a.190: and he urged that the opinion of the Fathers older than Augustine was to be embraced.
pass_a.191: For indeed from this time most of the Lutherans followed Hunnius, the Reformed for the most part constantly insisting upon the Augustinian Doctrine.
pass_a.192: Our men (says the often-praised Calixtus), from among whom formerly many likewise approved the Absolute Decree, gradually withdrew themselves to the Sentence of the first Four Centuries (namely, a Decree made according to foreknowledge), in which matter Aegidius Hunnius labored much and outstandingly:
pass_a.193: But it is difficult to propose this Sentence thus, so that it may not seem to have something akin to Pelagianism — just as indeed both Daniel Tossanus the Calvinist and Adam Tanner the Jesuit accuse Hunnius of Pelagianism. In the place cited, number 22. Compare the same Calixtus's Consideration of Reformed Doctrine according to the Thorun Confession, on Grace, p. 62.
pass_a.194: meanwhile judging neither this, nor any of the preceding Dissensus, to be Fundamental — in the earlier Tractate from number 23 to 35, number 45, and from number 76 to 82 inclusive.

189: §. VI. Not long after the Formula of Concord came into print — a story already more than familiar — the Dissensus hit its peak.

Aegidius Hunnius struck at the Predestination teaching that, from Augustine onward, had been all but the rule of the Western Church, and that the first Reformers on both Protestant sides had taken over: Luther and Zwingli, as pupils of Augustine and of Thomas Aquinas.
190: He pressed for taking up the view held by the Fathers who came before Augustine.
191: From then on the greater part of the Lutherans went with Hunnius, while most of the Reformed held fast to Augustinian teaching on this point.
192: As the often-praised Calixtus puts it: many of our own once approved the Absolute Decree as well, then by degrees fell back to the teaching of the first four centuries — a decree framed according to foreknowledge — and Aegidius Hunnius did a great and distinguished work in that change:
193: Still, it is hard to set out that teaching without seeming to shade toward Pelagianism — and Daniel Tossanus the Calvinist and Adam Tanner the Jesuit both charge Hunnius with Pelagianism (cited place, no. 22).
See also the same Calixtus, Consideration of Reformed Doctrine according to the Thorun Confession, on Grace, p. 62.
194: And they still did not count this split — or any of the earlier ones — as Fundamental: see the earlier Tractate, nos. 23–35, no. 45, and nos. 76–82 inclusive.
